newsitem.title: UK: UK Nobel prize economist an academic's academic.
newsitem.headline: UK Nobel prize economist an academic's academic.

text.p: British professor James Mirrlees, joint winner of the 1996 Nobel Prize for Economics, is a leading theorist and an academic's academic, economists said on Tuesday.
Mirrlees, who teaches at the University of Cambridge in England, shared the prize with Canadian William Vickrey. He told Reuters he was "full of glee" at winning the prize.

"He is a leading economic theorist on a wide range of issues," said Martin Weale, director of the National Institute For Economic and Social Research and one of the British Treasury's panel of independent advisers.
"He's avoided macro-forecasting, so he's not as well known as some economists in this country, but he is one of the country's leading economic theorists."
Weale, who once had offices next to Mirrlees at Cambridge, described Mirrlees, 50, as a "slightly austere Scotsman but an extraordinarily nice person."

The self-effacing economist has produced work on the concept of national income and optimal tax structures and how they should be set. But he won't forecast Britain's inflation next year, for example.
So outside the academic world, his name remains known to only a handful of people.
"He probably has the highest status among graduate students and the profession of anybody I've ever met," said an economist at the London Business School, who had also worked with Mirrlees.

He singled out a book co-written by Mirrlees concerning investment in uncertain circumstances. "His book on project appraisal became almost the bible for people looking to invest in developing countries."

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said they were awarding Myrrlees and Vickrey the $1.12 million prize "for their fundamental contributions to the economic theory of incentives under assymetric information."

In plainer English Vickrey, who is 82, produced research on different types of auctions and how they can be designed to maximise economic efficiency. Some 25 years later, Mirrlees built on Vickrey's work to relate it to tax systems.
